title: Lakhs March to Parliament Over NEET Paper Leak as Sonam Wangchuk's Hunger Strike Enters Day 23
excerpt: Tens of thousands of protesters clashed with police in New Delhi on the opening day of Parliament's monsoon session, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over India's worst exam scandal in years.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Hundreds of thousands protested in New Delhi, targeting Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over NEET paper leak.
  • Police used tear gas and batons, resulting in over 100 injuries during the protests.
  • Activist Sonam Wangchuk, on a hunger strike for 23 days, was forcibly hospitalized but vows to continue fasting.
  • CJP leaders demanded Pradhan's resignation and compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

Protest details from various news sources.
  • Hundreds of thousands of protesters marched toward Parliament on July 20, making it one of the largest demonstrations against the Modi government in years.
  • Police fired tear gas, used batons on crowds, barricaded metro stations and shut down mobile internet across parts of New Delhi; over 100 people were injured.
  • Activist Sonam Wangchuk, on day 23 of his hunger strike, was forcibly moved to Safdarjung Hospital and vows to continue fasting until student leaders can meet lawmakers.
  • CJP leaders met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda and submitted demands including Pradhan's resignation and Rs 1 crore compensation for families of 20-plus NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

A March That Shook the Capital

Hundreds of thousands of students, activists and unemployed youth poured into central New Delhi on Monday, July 20, in what the Wall Street Journal called "one of the biggest demonstrations to have faced Prime Minister Narendra Modi in years." The target: Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, whom protesters hold responsible for the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak that upended the futures of 2.27 million medical aspirants.

The "Chalo Sansad" march, organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was timed to coincide with the opening day of Parliament's monsoon session. Protesters gathered at Jantar Mantar before dawn and surged toward Parliament chanting, "We asked for 'Make in India,' you gave us 'Leak in India,'" according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Tear Gas, Batons and an Internet Shutdown

"Photo: Wikimedia Commons" style="max-width:100%;border-radius:8px" loading="lazy"><figcaption style="font-size:0.85rem;color:#666;margin-top:8px">Prime Minister Narendra Modi."

Delhi Police barricaded arterial roads, sealed metro station exits and jammed mobile internet. Officers fired at least 10-12 tear gas shells and lathi-charged crowds attempting to breach barricades near Parliament, according to Careers360. More than 50 police personnel and over 50 protesters were injured. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was briefly detained. The All India Students' Association alleged male officers used batons on women protesters.

"We did not lie to our families and come here to be picked up and detained like criminals."

— Anshika, 17, protester from Delhi's Badarpur

Wangchuk Extends His Fast

The march was galvanized by the forced hospitalization of Sonam Wangchuk, the 59-year-old Ladakh-based activist fasting since June 28. Police moved him to Safdarjung Hospital on July 18, citing deteriorating health. According to Reuters, Wangchuk has lost about 9 kg (20 pounds). In a handwritten note shared by his wife Gitanjali Angmo, he vowed to continue fasting until student leaders can meet parliamentarians, describing his confinement as "illegal detention."

From Meme to Mass Movement

The CJP began as an online meme in May after a judge reportedly called unemployed youth "cockroaches" and "parasites." It has since become a political force, drawing support from opposition politicians, Bollywood figures including Shabana Azmi and Prakash Raj, and students from Itanagar to Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar.

Government Response to Protests
›Police fired 10-12 tear gas shells.
›Metro stations were barricaded and mobile internet shut down.
›CJP leaders met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda.
›Parliament sessions disrupted multiple times.

CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on Monday with three demands: Pradhan's resignation, Wangchuk's release, and Rs 1 crore compensation for families of more than 20 NEET aspirants who have died by suicide. Nadda said the demands would be "discussed at the appropriate level" but made no commitments.

"Our demands are clear. The youth have gathered in huge numbers. We shall win!"

— Saurav Das, CJP spokesperson, on X

Parliament Paralyzed

Both houses were disrupted. The Rajya Sabha was adjourned six times after Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge rose to speak on the paper leak. Outside, Modi did not directly address the demands. "Parliament must function, meaningful discussions must take place," he said. "This is the demand of the times and the aspiration of the youth."

How the Crisis Unfolded

The scandal traces to the NEET-UG exam on May 3, when a "guess paper" circulated through WhatsApp in Rajasthan coaching centers matched up to 120 questions from the real exam. The NTA cancelled the exam on May 12 and the CBI arrested several insiders, including Pune-based professor P.V. Kulkarni, who allegedly dictated leaked questions for fees of Rs 2-10 lakh per student. A re-examination was held June 21, with the Indian Air Force transporting question papers to prevent another leak.

The NEET Scandal Timeline

NEET-UG exam held; leaked questions circulated.
May 12
Exam cancelled due to leaks.
June 21
Re-examination conducted.
July 18
Sonam Wangchuk hospitalized.

What Comes Next

Wangchuk remains hospitalized, monitored by teams from Safdarjung and AIIMS. The CJP has vowed continued agitation until Pradhan resigns. Parliament's monsoon session has begun with NEET dominating the opposition's agenda, and the Delhi High Court is hearing Wangchuk's wife's appeal to transfer him to a private hospital. For Indian families abroad with children aspiring to medical seats, the crisis has deepened skepticism about the reliability of India's national testing infrastructure.
